domain: Public Health Policy / Criminal Justice / Political Economy
topic_summary: Analysis of drug policy frameworks as contested readings of a substance-control kernel. Three dominant readings—prohibition, harm-reduction, and legalization—instantiate structurally different constraints with distinct victim sets, enforcement mechanisms, and extractiveness profiles. The kernel is the shared commitment to 'legitimate state authority over psychoactive substance access'; readings differ on what legitimates that authority and who bears costs.

key_entities: Substance users (criminalized under prohibition, medicalized under harm-reduction)
Medical/public health institutions (treatment providers, supervised consumption sites)
Pharmaceutical industry (legal opioid manufacturers, cannabis corporations)
Third-party victims (overdose deaths, impaired driving casualties, families)
Carceral system (prisons, probation, criminal records infrastructure)
Tax revenue apparatus (excise taxes on legal substances)
key_tensions: Individual autonomy vs paternalistic protection (user rights vs state intervention)
Public health framing vs criminal justice framing (treatment vs punishment)
Black market violence vs legal market extraction (cartel profits vs corporate profits)
key_mechanisms: Harm-reduction service provision (needle exchange, supervised consumption, naloxone distribution)
Legal market regulation (licensing, taxation, quality control)
key_absences: Indigenous/traditional use frameworks (peyote, ayahuasca, coca leaf—exempted or criminalized inconsistently)
Class/race disparities in enforcement (crack vs powder cocaine sentencing, stop-and-frisk targeting)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: Legitimate state authority to regulate psychoactive substance access and use
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: State claims interpretive monopoly over what constitutes 'legitimate control'—grounded variously in moral paternalism, public health expertise, or individual liberty

readings.commitment: Substance use is inherently harmful; state authority derives from moral duty to prevent harm through criminalization
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users enter victim set via criminalization; high carceral extractiveness; black market violence externality

readings.commitment: Substance use is a public health issue; state authority derives from duty to minimize harm without criminalization
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users medicalized not criminalized; moderate extractiveness via treatment mandates; persistent black market

readings.commitment: Competent adults have autonomy over substance use; state authority limited to preventing third-party harm
readings.expected_structural_delta: Users exit victim set; third-party harms (impaired driving, secondhand exposure) become primary constraint; corporate extractiveness via legal market

axes.structural_delta: State criminalizes substance possession/use; users become victims of carceral system; enforcement targets supply and demand via arrest/incarceration
axes.primary_observable: Incarceration rates for drug offenses; arrest rates; criminal record prevalence; black market violence metrics
axes.selection_reason: First reading: establishes baseline constraint where users are primary victims via criminalization

axes.structural_delta: State decriminalizes use but maintains control via medical gatekeeping; users medicalized not criminalized; black market persists for non-medical access
axes.primary_observable: Overdose death rates; HIV/Hepatitis C transmission rates; supervised consumption site utilization; treatment mandate prevalence
axes.selection_reason: Second reading: structurally distinct victim set (medicalized vs criminalized); different extractiveness profile

axes.human_readable: Legalization Reading (Autonomy with Third-Party Harm Limits)
axes.structural_delta: State permits adult use with regulatory controls; users exit victim set; third-party harms (impaired driving, youth access) become primary constraint; corporate market replaces black market
axes.primary_observable: Legal market size; tax revenue; impaired driving rates; youth use prevalence; corporate consolidation metrics
axes.selection_reason: Third reading: victim set shifts entirely to third parties; extractiveness shifts from state carceral to corporate profit

axes.structural_delta: Prohibition enforcement disproportionately targets marginalized communities despite similar use rates across demographics
axes.primary_observable: Arrest rates by race/class; sentencing disparities (crack vs powder cocaine); stop-and-frisk data
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: structurally downstream of prohibition_reading; captured as enforcement mechanism within that reading

axes.structural_delta: Prohibition creates lucrative black markets; violence emerges from lack of legal dispute resolution; harm-reduction partially reduces but does not eliminate
axes.primary_observable: Homicide rates in drug-trafficking regions; cartel revenue; turf war casualties
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: important externality but captured within prohibition/harm-reduction readings as enforcement mechanism consequence

axes.human_readable: Indigenous Traditional Use Exemption (Cultural Rights vs Universal Prohibition)
axes.structural_delta: Some jurisdictions exempt indigenous ceremonial use (peyote, ayahuasca) from prohibition; reveals cultural relativism in kernel interpretation
axes.primary_observable: Legal exemptions for religious/traditional use; prosecution rates for indigenous vs non-indigenous users
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: low centrality; reveals kernel instability but does not constitute independent reading

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Prohibition enforcement disproportionately targets marginalized communities
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Captured as enforcement mechanism within prohibition_reading; structurally downstream

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Prohibition creates black markets generating violence externalities
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Important consequence but captured within prohibition/harm-reduction readings as enforcement mechanism outcome

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Cultural/religious exemptions reveal kernel interpretation instability
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Low centrality; reveals kernel contestation but does not constitute independent reading

omegas.description: Why are alcohol and tobacco (higher mortality) legal while cannabis/psychedelics (lower mortality) prohibited? Reveals kernel is not grounded in harm metrics but in historical/cultural contingency. Prohibition reading claims universal harm principle but applies selectively.

Legal pharmaceutical opioids (OxyContin) created addiction epidemic, driving users to black market heroin/fentanyl. Legalization reading assumes legal market eliminates black market, but prescription system shows legal/illegal markets can coexist and feed each other.

Harm-reduction reading often conflates decriminalization (no criminal penalty for possession) with legalization (legal regulated market). These are structurally distinct: decriminalization leaves black market intact, legalization replaces it. Harm-reduction may be transitional reading, not stable endpoint.

Legalization reading assumes regulatory controls prevent corporate extractiveness, but tobacco/alcohol/gambling industries show regulatory capture is common. Legal cannabis market may replicate Big Tobacco playbook (youth marketing, addiction maximization, lobbying against public health measures).
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + deferred axis analysis

omegas.description: Emerging fourth reading: psychedelic-assisted therapy (psilocybin, MDMA for PTSD). Medical legitimacy without recreational legalization. Potentially distinct reading with different victim set (patients denied access vs recreational users criminalized), but insufficient structural independence from harm-reduction reading to warrant separate generation.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel structure confirmed: three readings emit genuinely different constraints with distinct victim sets (criminalized users vs medicalized users vs third-party harm victims). Extractiveness shifts from carceral to medical to corporate across readings. Readings are structurally independent and non-collapsible.
